Spices
spī´sĕz
n. pl. (aromatic substances used in anointing, incense, and burial; rendering Hebrew besem, Greek arōma)
From Latin species, a kind or sort, hence goods of value. In Scripture spices are costly, fragrant, and always associated with consecration or with death.

Biblical Definition

Spices in Scripture are costly aromatics, and they mark the two solemn places: the sanctuary and the grave. God specified them for the holy anointing oil by name and weight: “Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much… and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels” (Exo 30:23) — the recipe given, not invented, and reserved on pain of being cut off. The Song gathers them as the imagery of the beloved's garden: “Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices” (Son 4:14). And the women carried them to a tomb: “when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him” (Mar 16:1) — love's last service, prepared for a body that was no longer there. The spices of the sanctuary consecrate; the spices of the tomb honour the dead; and on Easter morning the second use was made gloriously unnecessary.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines spice as a vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell and pungent to the taste, used in sauces and in medicine — and figuratively a small quantity.

expand to see more

SPICE, n. A vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell, and pungent to the taste; used in sauces and in cookery.

2. A small quantity; something that enriches or alters the quality of a thing in a small degree.

SPICE, v.t. To season with spice, or with aromatic substances.

SPICERY, n. Spices in general; also, a repository of spices.

Key Scripture

Exo 30:23 — "Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels,"

Son 4:14 — "Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:"

Mar 16:1 — "And when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him."

Lev 23:36 — "Seven days ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD: on the eighth day shall be an holy convocation unto you; and ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD: it is a solemn assembly; and ye shall do no servile work therein."

Modern Corruption

The holy anointing oil was a compounded formula God fenced from common use, and the modern appetite for anointing oils, sacred scents, and atmosphere-as-worship runs directly against the fence.

expand to see more

Exodus 30 does not merely list ingredients; it forbids replication. Whosoever compounded any like it, or put any of it upon a stranger, was to be cut off from his people. God gave the recipe and then closed it, because the fragrance signified a consecration He alone conferred. Modern religious commerce reopens it — anointing oils sold by the vial, sacred scents marketed for prayer rooms, atmosphere manufactured and then credited to the Spirit. The regulative principle applies to the nose as much as to the ear: what God has not commanded in worship is not ours to add.

The spices of Mark 16 point the better way. The women were doing the last kindness available to the dead, and it was a genuine kindness, bought at cost, carried at dawn. That they found no body to anoint is the gospel: the fragrance prepared for a corpse was left unused because the corpse was risen. Christian devotion is not less than theirs in love; it is simply relieved of the errand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew besem (H1314), balsam, spice, sweet odour; Greek arōma (G759), fragrant spices for embalming — the sanctuary and the sepulchre.

expand to see more

Hebrew besem (H1314) — balsam, spice, sweet smell; the principal spices of the anointing oil (Exo 30:23).

Hebrew sammim (H5561) — sweet spices for the holy incense (Exo 30:34), likewise fenced from common use.

Greek arōma (G759) — spices, aromatics used in burial; the sweet spices of Mar 16:1.

Usage

"“Take thou also unto thee principal spices” — a recipe given by God and closed to imitation."

"“With all the chief spices” — the garden imagery of the Song."

"“Had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him” — a kindness the resurrection made unnecessary."
